title: Unit Key Equations and Key Terms

children.text: A type of radioactive decay in which an unstable nucleus emits an alpha particle (consisting of two protons and two neutrons) and transforms into a new nucleus with a lower atomic number and mass number.
A high-energy helium nucleus consisting of two protons and two neutrons, resulting from the loss of two electrons from a helium atom. It is commonly emitted during radioactive decay processes.
Region on a graph of proton number versus neutron number containing all the stable (nonradioactive) nuclides; also called the zone, belt, or valley of stability.
SI unit of radioactivity; 1 Bq represents a rate of radioactive decay equal to 1 disintegration/s.

A type of radioactive decay in which an unstable nucleus transforms by emitting a beta particle. Beta decay results in the change of the atomic number of the nucleus without a significant change in its mass number.
A medical treatment similar to internal radiation therapy, but chemical rather than radioactive substances are introduced into the body to kill cancer cells.

A three-part structure of materials that protects the exterior of a nuclear fission reactor and operating personnel from the high temperatures, pressures, and radiation levels inside the reactor. Also called a shield.
Material inserted into the fuel assembly that absorbs neutrons and can be raised or lowered to adjust the rate of a fission reaction.

The minimum amount of fissile material needed to maintain a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. Below this mass, the chain reaction will not be sustained, and above it, the reaction can increase exponentially.
A  unit for rate of radioactive decay frequently used in medicine; 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10
The nuclide that is produced as a result of the radioactive decay of a parent nuclide. It may itself be stable or may undergo further radioactive decay.

A process in which an unstable nucleus captures an inner orbital electron and combines it with a proton to form a neutron and a neutrino. This decreases the atomic number by 1 without changing the mass number, often leaving the daughter nuclide in an excited state.
Describes a material that can sustain a nuclear fission chain reaction when struck by a thermal (slow) neutron. Common fissile materials include uranium-235, plutonium-239, and uranium-233.

A nuclear reaction in which a heavy atomic nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, along with the release of a large amount of energy, neutrons, and gamma radiation. This process is commonly used in nuclear reactors and atomic bombs.
An atom, molecule, or ion that has at least one unpaired valence electron.
The combination of very light nuclei into heavier nuclei, accompanied by the conversion of mass into large amounts of energy.
A nuclear reactor in which fusion reactions of light nuclei are controlled.
A short wavelength, high-energy electromagnetic radiation that exhibits wave-particle duality.

A type of radioactive decay in which an excited nucleus releases excess energy in the form of gamma rays, which are high-energy photons. This process does not change the atomic number or mass number of the nucleus but brings the nucleus to a lower energy state. Gamma emission often accompanies other forms of decay, such as alpha or beta decay.
An instrument that detects and measures radiation via the ionization produced in a Geiger-Müller tube.
SI unit for measuring ionizing radiation dose; 1 Gy corresponds to 1 J of energy absorbed per kg of tissue.

The time required for half of the nuclei in a sample of a radioactive substance to undergo decay, reducing the number of radioactive atoms by half. It is a measure of the rate at which a radioactive substance transforms into a more stable form.
Subatomic particles or electromagnetic waves with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms or molecules, causing them to form ions.
Atoms of the same element that have different masses due to different numbers of neutrons.
A number of protons or neutrons corresponding to a complete shell of nuclear energy levels and a particularly stable nucleus; common magic numbers are 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, and 126.
The difference between the actual mass of an atomic nucleus and the sum of the masses of its individual protons and neutrons; occurs due to the conversion of mass into binding energy.
Equation demonstrating that mass and energy are interchangeable:
A unit for rate of radioactive decay frequently used in medicine; 1 mCi = 3.7 × 10
Electromagnetic waves with insufficient energy to remove electrons from atoms or molecules; it only excites electrons or speeds up the movement of atoms or molecules.
The energy required to disassemble a nucleus into its separate protons and neutrons (or the energy released when the nucleus is formed from its constituent nucleons).
The study of the structure of atomic nuclei and the processes that cause changes in nuclear structure.

Material that can be consumed to release energy through nuclear fission or fusion. In nuclear reactors, common nuclear fuels include uranium-235 and plutonium-239, which undergo fission to produce heat used to generate electricity.
A substance that slows neutrons to a speed low enough to cause fission.

A process involving changes to a nucleus that result in alterations to the atomic number, mass number, or energy state. These reactions can include fusion, fission, and radioactive decay, and are often accompanied by the release or absorption of significant amounts of energy.
A system that harnesses energy from nuclear fission by maintaining a controlled chain reaction. It safely manages the release of energy to produce electricity or heat or for scientific research.
A substance (usually water) that circulates through a nuclear reactor to transfer or remove heat.

The process of changing one element or isotope into another through nuclear reactions or radioactive decay. This change can occur naturally, as in radioactive decay series, or be induced artificially in nuclear reactors or particle accelerators.
A collective term for the protons and neutrons within a nucleus.
The nucleus of a particular isotope, characterized by a specific number of protons and neutrons.
The original unstable nuclide that undergoes radioactive decay to form a different nuclide, known as the daughter nuclide.
A device that uses electric and magnetic fields to increase the kinetic energy of charged particles, such as nuclei, for use in transmutation reactions and various scientific research applications.
An antiparticle to the electron, possessing identical properties to an electron except for having a positive charge instead of a negative one.

A type of beta decay in which an unstable nucleus emits a positron (the antimatter counterpart of an electron) and a neutrino. This process occurs when a proton in the nucleus is converted into a neutron. Positron emission decreases the atomic number by 1 while the mass number remains unchanged.
A unit used for measuring ionizing radiation dose; 1 rad = 0.01 Gy.
A device that measures ionizing radiation and is used to determine personal radiation exposure.
The use of high-energy radiation to damage the DNA of cancer cells, which kills them or keeps them from dividing.

The spontaneous process by which an unstable atomic nucleus loses energy by emitting radiation in the form of particles or electromagnetic waves. This can result in the transformation of the original atom into a different element or a different isotope of the same element.

A sequence of radioactive decays that certain isotopes undergo until they reach a stable nuclide. Each step involves the transformation of a parent nuclide into a daughter nuclide, which may itself be radioactive and continue decaying until stability is achieved.
A radioisotope used to track or follow a substance by monitoring its radioactive emissions. Also called radioactive label.

The spontaneous emission of particles or electromagnetic radiation from the unstable nucleus of an atom as it transforms into a more stable form. This process can involve the emission of alpha particles, beta particles, or gamma rays.

A method for dating objects up to about 50,000 years old that were derived from once-living matter. It measures the ratio of carbon-14 (¹⁴C) to carbon-12 (¹²C) in the object and compares it to the ratio in the present-day atmosphere. This technique relies on the known half-life of ¹⁴C to calculate the time since the organism's death.
A radioactive isotope of an element; it has an unstable nucleus and emits radiation as it decays to a more stable form.

A technique used to determine the age of materials such as rocks or carbon by measuring the relative proportions of specific radioactive isotopes and their decay products. This method relies on the known half-lives of these isotopes to calculate the time elapsed since the material was formed.
A ratio of the effect of one type of radiation on tissue compared to a standard, if both have the same absorbed energy.
A unit for radiation damage, frequently used in medicine; 100 rem = 1 Sv.
An instrument that uses a scintillator—a material that emits light when excited by ionizing radiation—to detect and measure radiation.
SI unit representing the health risk caused by ionizing radiation; it depends on the amount of energy absorbed, the type of radiation, and the type of tissue.
The force of attraction between nucleons (protons and neutrons) that holds the nucleus together, overcoming the repulsive force between positively charged protons.

An amount of fissile material that is insufficient to sustain a nuclear chain reaction. In this state, the reaction rate decreases over time because the number of neutrons produced is less than the number needed to maintain the reaction.

An amount of fissile material that exceeds the critical mass, leading to an increasing rate of nuclear chain reactions. In this state, the reaction rate accelerates, potentially resulting in an explosive release of energy if uncontrolled.
The bombardment of one type of nuclei with other nuclei or neutrons.
Elements with an atomic number greater than 92; these elements do not occur in nature.
